title: Vishing, smishing and voice deepfakes
body_md:
## A phone call proves nothing

You are at the front door with a shopping bag in each hand when the phone buzzes: your bank, a courier, or a voice that sounds exactly like your nephew. That is the moment these scams are built for, when your hands are full and your mind is elsewhere. **Smishing** is phishing by text; **vishing** is phishing by voice. A text can borrow the name of a delivery company or a bank, and a caller can claim to be an investigator, an executive, a relative. The sender name, the number on the screen, a familiar voice, even a second message that matches the first all count for little when the contact began out of nowhere.

A fake delivery text often carries a short link, though not always, and a readable web address can still lead to a lookalike page. So judge the request. Open the delivery company’s app, or type its address yourself, and see whether the package has a problem at all. Expecting a package makes the text more believable, but it does not make it real. Genuine services do send texts with links, and not every link is a trap; for anything consequential, though, use a route you chose yourself.

On a call the usual order is authority (“the security team”), then fear (“your money is at risk”), then an instant fix (“stay with me and move it”). A cloned voice can make a call from a relative or a boss feel personal. The FTC warns that a short clip of someone speaking can be enough to imitate a relative. You do not have to judge whether the audio is genuine. Hang up on the incoming call and reach the person on a number you already stored; if they don’t answer, try someone else you trust. For a transfer at work, use the usual approval channel and a colleague you know, not the email that turned up alongside the call.

### The route has to be yours

Switching channels helps only when the new route is **independent**. Calling back the number your caller ID shows, the number in the text, or one the speaker gives you keeps you inside their story. It is like asking a man selling a watch to confirm the receipt he printed himself. Make sure the suspicious call has really ended, or use a different phone. If you tapped a link but typed nothing, close it and check with the service itself. If you entered a password or paid, go to the service’s verified recovery channel promptly. Keep any real message, code or URL out of the exercises below.

With text or with voice, do the same thing: work out which organization is supposed to be speaking, then get to it yourself.

widget_config.goal: When an unexpected text or call asks you for something, switch to a contact route you chose before it arrived.
widget_config.today_action: From your home screen, open a delivery or banking app and find its help page or transaction history, so you know the way before an alert arrives.
widget_config.scope: General advice on choosing a safe channel. The FTC examples come from the US, and the NCSC reporting routes apply in the UK. Voice cloning is possible, but it should not be assumed in every odd call.

sources.title: UK NCSC: how to spot a scam message or call
sources.scope: British public guidance, published in 2021 and reviewed in 2022. Warning signs and independent contact: cues to weigh, not a test that gives a verdict.

sources.title: US FTC: fake delivery texts
sources.scope: A US example involving USPS (April 2025). Check the delivery yourself instead of using the links you were sent.

sources.title: US FTC: fake family emergencies
sources.scope: US consumer guidance (2023) on voice cloning, demands for secrecy and getting in touch with family directly.

sources.title: US FTC: unexpected calls about money at risk
sources.scope: US consumer alert (January 2026). Call back using the number on your card or statement, your app or the official site.

blocks.title: A package text that arrives on time
blocks.situation: You are expecting a package. A text says an address field failed and asks for a small redelivery fee on a linked page. The sender name looks like the delivery company’s.
blocks.analysis: The timing and the branding make it believable, and that is exactly what the trick relies on. Open the delivery company’s app yourself, or use the tracking number from your original order. If something is wrong, you can fix it there. Don’t follow the link or enter card details just because the fee is small.

blocks.title: A reminder from the clinic
blocks.situation: A clinic you use sends a text with nothing but an appointment time, and says you can change it in your existing patient portal. You open the portal from a bookmark you saved long ago and see the same appointment.
blocks.analysis: This looks like a genuine text. The same appointment, in a portal you opened by your own route, backs it up. Keep or change the booking there; there is no reason to answer the text with medical or payment details.

blocks.title: Two channels, one claim
blocks.setup: You work at an invented community center, and everything in this exercise, names and accounts included, is made up. The first two decisions belong to one attempt to get a payment out of you by text and by phone. The third is a new invoice that starts from scratch; nothing you chose earlier carries over.

steps.prompt: A text carries a supplier’s link and says the invoice expires at noon. What first?

choices.text: Open the center’s own purchasing system and look for the invoice.
choices.consequence: You find out whether the claim exists anywhere outside the message.
choices.explanation: A real deadline will show up in the usual records.

choices.text: Open the link. The center does have a supplier.
choices.consequence: Having a supplier proves nothing about this invoice or about where the money would go.
choices.explanation: Use an invoice or a system you reach independently.

steps.prompt: A caller who sounds like your manager repeats the exact invoice amount. What next?

choices.text: Approve the payment. Two channels now agree.
choices.consequence: Both channels could be run by one attacker, or fed by the same information.
choices.explanation: Details that match and a voice you know are still not independent approval.

choices.text: Follow the center’s normal approval process and message your manager’s saved work account.
choices.consequence: You ask for a separate check on both the person and the payment.
choices.explanation: A genuine manager would expect the usual process to be followed.

steps.prompt: A new invoice. You open the center’s purchasing system yourself. A note in your manager’s saved work account confirms the supplier is genuine. Then a text arrives saying the supplier’s bank details have changed, with new ones attached. Nothing is approved yet. What now?

choices.text: Hold the payment and ask purchasing to confirm the new account with the supplier through its existing contact.
choices.consequence: The changed account gets a check of its own.
choices.explanation: A genuine supplier can confirm through a contact you already held; until it does, don’t pay.

choices.text: Pay the new account. Your manager has confirmed the supplier is genuine.
choices.consequence: The supplier is real, but the account number came from a text nobody has checked.
choices.explanation: A change of recipient needs independent verification with the supplier, under your workplace’s policy.

blocks.debrief: A text and a familiar-sounding call can prop up the same false request. The last invoice, a separate one, hides its problem in a changed recipient, even though your manager has vouched for the supplier. If you approved the first payment, go straight to the center’s verified reporting route. Replay the decisions and check before you approve.

questions.prompt: A text from a sender name you recognize includes a readable web address for the delivery company. What is safest when it asks for payment?

choices.text: Open the delivery company’s app or site by a route you already use.
choices.explanation: A believable name or address does not verify the request.

choices.text: Pay through the link, since it isn’t shortened.
choices.explanation: A long address can mislead too, or be copied.

questions.prompt: A relative’s voice asks for urgent help, but their saved number doesn’t answer. What is the best next step?

choices.text: Send the money. The voice is unmistakable.
choices.explanation: A familiar sound does not establish who is speaking.

choices.text: Contact another trusted relative, or reach them by some other route you know, before sending anything.
choices.explanation: A second, independent person can help you check a real emergency.

questions.prompt: A genuine clinic reminder matches the appointment in the portal you opened yourself. What follows?

choices.text: Use the portal for any change. The text need not be treated as fraud.
choices.explanation: A match in a portal you opened independently bears out an ordinary reminder.

choices.text: The reminder must be malicious, because it came by SMS.
choices.explanation: A channel alone cannot classify a message.
